card.stem: A front porch projects 1.2 metres from the external wall of a dwelling house, as shown. The insulated wall of the porch is of timber frame construction with a rainscreen of vertical cedar cladding. The studwork is 250 mm × 50 mm. The external wall of the house is a 400 mm rendered concrete block wall with a full-fill insulated cavity. The lean-to roof of the porch is an insulated slated roof and has a pitch of 30°. Insulated plasterboard is also fixed to the underside of the sloping rafters.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the porch showing the external wall of the porch, the sloping roof, and the front wall of the house. Show the typical construction details of the porch from a point 300 mm below the wallplate, through the sloping rafters to a level 300 mm above and 200 mm below the abutment of the roof and the front wall of the house. Show three courses of slate at eaves. It is not necessary to show window or door details.

rows.contextNote: Best four details, 4 each. Such as: external and internal renders; 100 mm block leaves with wall ties; full-fill insulated cavity; lintels; thermal blocks below the roof abutment; a timber bearer or metal hanger on the main wall; any four dimensions.

Best four details, 4 each. Such as: slate on 35 × 50 mm counter battens and battens; breathable membrane on 10 mm OSB; 250–300 mm rafters or I-joists packed with 300 mm insulation; insulated plasterboard with vapour control layer; tilting fillet and ventilation at eaves and roof head; fascia, soffit and gutter.

Best four details, 4 each. Such as: double joists at the head; cedar cladding on battens and counter battens; breather membrane on 10 mm OSB; 250 × 50 mm studs with 250 mm breathable insulation; OSB with taped vapour control layer inside; insulated 38 mm service cavity; 12.5 mm plasterboard; airtightness tapes.
Scale 4 and drafting 4, each excellent 4, good 3, fair 2.

card.stem: A house built in the 1970s has an uninsulated solid concrete ground floor, as shown, with a sand/cement fine screed finish.
card.questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the uninsulated concrete ground floor, given the following data: Sand/cement fine screed thickness 50 mm; Concrete floor slab thickness 100 mm; Radon barrier thickness 0.25 mm; Sand blinding thickness 40 mm; Hardcore thickness 200 mm; Subsoil thickness 300 mm.
Thermal data of the concrete ground floor: Resistance of internal top surface of floor (R) 0.104 m2 °C/W; Resistivity of fine screed (r) 0.710 m °C/W; Conductivity of concrete floor slab (k) 1.280 W/m °C; Conductivity of radon barrier (k) 0.250 W/m °C; Conductivity of sand blinding (k) 0.160 W/m °C; Conductivity of hardcore (k) 1.350 W/m °C; Conductivity of subsoil (k) 1.600 W/m °C.

rows.contextNote: The calculation set out in a table of material, conductivity, resistivity, thickness and resistance.

rows.verbatim: Internal top surface resistance Fine screed Concrete floor slab Radon barrier Sand blinding Hardcore Subsoil
rows.contextNote: Seven resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the screed): internal top surface 0.1040 (given); screed 0.05 × 0.71 = 0.0355; slab 0.1/1.28 = 0.0781; radon barrier 0.00025/0.25 = 0.0010; sand blinding 0.04/0.16 = 0.2500; hardcore 0.2/1.35 = 0.1481; subsoil 0.3/1.6 = 0.1875. All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 0.8042 m²°C/W.

rows.verbatim: Calculation of U-value of ground floor
rows.contextNote: U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 0.8042 = 1.2434 W/m²°C, with units.

sourceMaterial.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Construction Studies 2018 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission.
sourceMaterial.presentationNote: All printed data are retained in the original question. Parts (b) and (c) use the U-value from (a); the scheme’s worked answers are U = 1.2434 W/m²°C, an annual cost of €352.50 and 216.9 mm of expanded polystyrene.

card.stem: Green design is about being green, rather than simply appearing to be green. So greening your house is about more than just buying all sorts of expensive ‘eco-bling’ and adding it to your house. Ironically, that could be just another display of consumerism. Rather, greening your house is about making responsible environmental choices based on what you want to do, what you can do and what you can afford. This means that - before we get into the minutiae of sustainable building materials - we should address some fundamentals, chief among which is the need to build modestly and source locally.
